verify:reader-as-adam.interpretationChallenges:
Strongest alternative (against I2 and I5): adam means NUMA literally. On the Xeon he ran die-against-die tests where a "die" was a sub-NUMA domain, so core and memory sat together in one domain and the device in another. He may assume the CRB shows one NUMA node per die and want the whole-path effect: host thread and its memory on the far die, device on the near die. Under this reading the draft is only partly sound. Its one-node sentence is the fact he needs. But the plan covers the core side only, the either/or question has no "both together" choice, and the reply hides that the firmware has a per-die NUMA mode. Adam would answer "both, can you enable NUMA?", which costs one more round. Naming the per-die NUMA firmware mode in the reply repairs this.

Second alternative (against I1): "extra" is relative to the single-die SoC he measured in June. He wants an absolute CRB number comparable to June (root complex, bus and die crossing), measured the same way with small CPU-to-PCIe writes. The die-against-die difference is then only part of the answer, and the access type must match June. The draft stays sound but "the same access" becomes the main gap. Insufficient data: the text does not say whether Jibin knows the June method.

Third alternative (against I4): message 3 is a loose suggestion to the group, or adam expects Jibin to pass it to Jacob, whom Jibin named for the IO path. The draft takes ownership through "Plan:". That is sound only if Jibin intends to do the work.

Against I5: the one-node mode already decides what can run without a firmware change (core-to-device only). The real decision for adam is whether the DMA case is worth a firmware mode change. The draft's question hides that trade.

I3 (the "extra die" is the other 64-core die, not a separate IO die) holds, given that each die has its own PCIe subsystems. Low risk.

Judgement of the step "So I can choose the die of the core, not the die of the memory": sound in the narrow sense that Linux with one NUMA node gives no way to place memory by die, and pinning a core works. (2) The limit is a firmware setting, not a fixed property: PER_CHIPLET_NUMA exists. (3) Only a user buffer was measured, no kernel IO or DMA buffer. (4) It hides the consequence that every IO buffer above 2 lines is homed on both dies, so the run on the device's own die is not free of die crossing.

draftProblems.phrase: So I can choose the die of the core, not the die of the memory.
draftProblems.problem: Not false for the board as it ran on Nov 17, but stated more firmly and more widely than the files allow. (1) The limit comes from a firmware setting, not from the board: the setting "NUMA Domain" offers PER_CHIPLET_NUMA (ifr.txt:14011), and Arm's own die-to-die tests require a two-node boot (Sys Diag guide page 37). (2) "Die of the memory" merges two things. The project record covers where a 64-byte line is homed in the cache system: by an address hash, half on each mesh (mesh0-or-mesh1.md:7). The same record says that which chiplet's DRAM holds a line was not resolved (mesh0-or-mesh1.md:203). (3) The record measured one 32 MiB user buffer. No kernel IO or DMA buffer was measured. (4) The sentence hides a consequence that changes how adam should read the result: every IO buffer larger than 2 lines has lines homed on both dies, so the run from the device's own die still has die-crossing traffic for the buffer. The comparison isolates the core side only. (5) "Die of the core" is backed by a file for NVMe only (phoenix-crb-host.md:21: the queue interrupt fires on the CPU that issued the IO, note of Oct 22). I found no saved record of which CPU services the USB controller's interrupt.
draftProblems.fix: "In UMA mode Linux cannot place memory on one die. Each 64-byte line is homed on die 0 or die 1 by an address hash, about half on each (measured on a user buffer). So I can vary only the die of the core. The firmware also has a per-chiplet NUMA mode, which needs a reboot; in that mode the memory die could be chosen too."

draftProblems.phrase: Which matters more: core-to-device access, or device DMA to memory?
draftProblems.problem: The second option cannot be tested as a die comparison in the mode the board ran in. The sentence before says the memory die cannot be chosen, so the question offers a choice the plan cannot deliver unless the firmware is switched to PER_CHIPLET_NUMA (ifr.txt:14011, needs a reboot of a shared machine). adam's own word is "NUMA-crossing", and Arm's die-to-die tests use the two-node mode (Sys Diag guide page 37), so he may expect that mode. Insufficient data: no file shows how memory or line homing is laid out in PER_CHIPLET_NUMA mode; a boot in that mode plus the home-mesh measurement would show it.
draftProblems.fix: "Which matters more: core-to-device access (I can test this now), or device DMA to memory (this needs the firmware switched to per-chiplet NUMA and a reboot)?"

draftProblems.problem: Supported as a list of installed devices (same 7 functions in all 12 saved boots), but the "or" hides facts that the files give. (1) By the address-map inference both NVMe drives are on die 0 (segments 0000 and 000b) and the USB controller (segment 0010) is the only installed device on die 1. For the USB controller no file states the die in words. (2) The two device kinds are not like for like. The USB controller is a TI TUSB73x0 xHCI controller on a x1 link with a capability of 5.0 GT/s (k-10.txt:2657 "capable of 4.000 Gb/s with 5.0 GT/s PCIe x1 link"). The NVMe on segment 0000 is the boot drive with the root filesystem on a 16 GT/s x1 link (k0.txt:958, :2311). The NVMe on segment 000b is the data drive in a x4 slot. (3) The Broadcom NIC (OCP card, segment 0007, die 0 group) is a further installed device and is not named. Hypothesis, not from a file: the die-crossing cost seen for memory is 56 to 59 ns per load (crb-memory-hierarchy.html:253), which may be too small to see inside one USB or NVMe request; no IO latency number for the CRB is in the files I read, and a first run would show the run-to-run spread.

draftProblems.problem: Supported as dated. Five boots of Nov 17 (03:48 to 05:45 UTC) show "Nodes=1" and all 17 PCI buses "on NUMA node 0" (k-4.txt to k0.txt). The firmware setting read UMA at 02:09 UTC and again at 20:27 UTC on Nov 17 (ifr.txt:14007-14008; firmware-snapshot-20261117/settings-forms-ifr.txt:10322-10325), and the SRAT table saved at 20:27 UTC has one proximity domain. Limit: no saved record is later than 2026-11-17 20:27 UTC, and today is Nov 20. The files cannot show the mode after that time. The sentence carries its date, so it is not over-stated; it should not be read as today's state.
draftProblems.fix: "The CRB was in UMA mode (one NUMA node) when I last checked on Nov 17."

draftProblems.phrase: First I will confirm which die each device connects to.
draftProblems.problem: The promise is firmer than the files allow. In UMA mode Linux reports NUMA node 0 for every PCI bus and proximity domain 0 for every SMMU (k0.txt:959-1605, :805-810), so the operating system cannot confirm the die. What exists is an address-map inference, already strong: the saved IORT table ties segments 0000 to 000e to SMMUs at 0x1c0000000 to 0x1d0000000 and segments 0010 to 001e to SMMUs 0x10_0000_0000 higher, the block that the boot log labels "chip number 1" for the GIC. Arm's guide gives words only for PSS0 ("Chip 0 PSS0", page 14). A real confirmation needs Arm's board map or a statement from adam.
draftProblems.fix: "From the address map, both NVMe drives look to be on die 0 and the USB controller on die 1. This is inferred, not documented. If you have the board's PCIe map, I will check it against that."

verify:file-facts.notes:
Short version: 6 of the 12 claims are confirmed as written (F1, F2, F3, F4, F8, F9). 6 are right in substance but need a wording change (F5, F6, F7, F10, F11, F12). No claim is refuted and no draft sentence is false; two draft sentences are stated more widely than the files allow.

Findings that matter most for the reply:
- The limit "cannot choose the memory die" is a firmware setting. The setting offers PER_CHIPLET_NUMA, and Arm's own die-to-die tests require a two-node boot. The draft presents the limit as fixed and then asks adam to choose an option (device DMA to memory) that the current mode cannot test.
- In UMA mode every buffer above 2 lines is homed on both dies. So the run from the device's own die is not a clean "no crossing" case. The record does not say which die's DDR holds the data.
- The Broadcom NIC is itself a plug-in card (OCP NIC 3.0 slot, PSS1), and it works. So "no add-in card" in F5 must be narrowed to the CEM slots.
- The segment-to-chip mapping is a strong inference with no counter-evidence. The 0x10_0000_0000 offset holds for GIC, ITS and SMMU, not for PCI ECAM or PCI memory windows. For PSS0 Arm's guide gives the chip in words ("Chip 0 PSS0"); for the USB controller nothing does.

Points on the interpretation (I1 to I5), outside the F list:
- I1, "the board loses power with any add-in card installed": I found no source for this wording in adam's messages or in the local files (searched notebook, machines/arm-crb, crb, the welcome kit docs). adam wrote "blocked by the power subsystem issue" and "fix from Arm for the PCIe card power". That can also mean the card gets no power. "Any add-in card" is too wide, because the OCP NIC card and two E1.S drives are installed and work. Unverified; only adam or the Slack history can settle it. I did not read Slack.
- I1, the name: Arm's guide (page 4) writes "Arm AGI CPU Reference Board". The word "customer" does not occur in the two PDFs I searched.
- I1 and I3, "64-core chiplet": each chip has 70 cores, 64 enabled (SMBIOS "Core Count: 140", "Core Enabled: 128"; phx_pwr_thermal_monitor.py:55 "NUM_OF_CLUSTERS = 70"). "64 cores per chip" is Arm's wording for this platform.
- I3, "not a separate IO die": supported. Each chip has its own 3 PCIe subsystems (inject_err.py:1947-1949), and no file names an IO die.
- I4, "possibly Jibin and William Baumann": no file checked; the name is not in the sources given.
- I2 and I5: Arm ties die-crossing tests to a two-node NUMA boot (Sys Diag guide page 37). adam's word "NUMA-crossing" may therefore mean that mode literally. The one question to adam may need to name the NUMA mode.

Other facts read during the check:
- The SVK user guide documents firmware 0.9.0; the CRB reported BIOS AGI-CPU-CRB-v0.7.2 on Nov 17. Hardware facts (two chips, PSS layout) match our own logs, but lists such as "validated devices" belong to 0.9.0. That list includes "ConnectX-8 card connected to the PSS4 and PSS0 Gen6 FHHL-slot controllers" (page 10), so Arm has run a card in the two x16 CEM slots, one per chip group.
- Latest saved state of the CRB in these files: 2026-11-17 20:27 UTC. Nothing later was checked; no remote login was made.

Method and limits:
- The Read tool could not render PDF pages (pdftoppm missing). I read the PDF text with PyMuPDF instead. Page numbers are PDF page numbers and match the printed "Page N of".
- ACPI tables (IORT, SRAT, SLIT, MADT, MCFG) from /home/jhan/workspace/machines/arm-crb/firmware-snapshot-20261117/acpi were decoded with small parsers I wrote. These tables come from the boot of Nov 17 about 20:02 UTC, a later boot than k0.txt.
- All counts were made with grep or scripts over all 12 files k0.txt and k-1.txt to k-11.txt.
- No project file was changed. No Slack message, email or canvas was sent or drafted.
